sections.h: The beginning of the revolt, 175–164 BC
sections.b:
1 Maccabees traces the revolt from Antiochus IV's accession in 175 BC through the Hellenizers' gymnasium, the robbing of the Temple (169 BC), the sack of Jerusalem and the building of the Citadel (167 BC), and the king's decree against the law, ending in the "abomination of desolation" on the altar in December 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:10–64). The revolt begins at Modein, when the priest Mattathias kills a Jew sacrificing at the king's altar and calls the zealous to follow him (1 Maccabees 2:15–28). After his death in 166 BC his son Judas wins at the pass of Beth-horon, at Emmaus and at Beth-zur, and in December 164 BC cleanses and rededicates the Temple (1 Maccabees 3:1–4:61).

2 Maccabees tells the same years with more about the high priests Jason and Menelaus and the martyrs, and without Mattathias. The two accounts differ on the order of Lysias's campaign and the rededication, and on whether Antiochus IV died before or after it.

common: The persecution under Antiochus IV and the first victories of Judas, about 167–164 BC, are generally accepted as historical, with the rededication of the Temple in December 164 BC.
uncommon: Elias Bickerman argued that the persecution was devised by Jerusalem's own Hellenizing leaders rather than by the king.

sections.b: 1 Maccabees begins its story of the crisis with "renegades" who urged a covenant with the nations, built a gymnasium in Jerusalem and hid their circumcision (1 Maccabees 1:11–15). 2 Maccabees names their leader as Jason, who bought the high priesthood and enrolled the citizens of Jerusalem as "Antiochenes," so that priests left the altar to watch the games (2 Maccabees 4:7–15). For both books, Greek ways are apostasy. Historians such as Tcherikover and Hengel describe a more complex world: Greek language and customs had been spreading in Judea for a century and a half, and many Jews who kept the law also spoke Greek and used Greek forms. The struggle the books describe was within Judaism as much as against a foreign king.

On 15 Kislev 145 of the Seleucid era (December 167 BC) the king's men "built an abomination of desolation on the altar" of the Temple, and ten days later they sacrificed on "the pagan altar that stood on top of the altar of sacrifice" (1 Maccabees 1:54–59). The book takes the phrase from Daniel without explaining it. Most scholars think the object was a Greek altar, perhaps with sacred stones, set over the altar of burnt offering, and 2 Maccabees 6:2 says the Temple was renamed for Olympian Zeus. Judas's men tore down the defiled altar three years later and built a new one (1 Maccabees 4:42–47).

common: Most scholars think Daniel 11:31 and 12:11 refer to the pagan altar set up in the Temple in 167 BC, described in 1 Maccabees 1:54.
uncommon: Some dispensationalist interpreters hold that Daniel 9:27 and Matthew 24:15 describe a future idol in a rebuilt temple, and that Antiochus's altar was only a preview.

sections.b: After the victory at Beth-zur, Judas and his brothers went up to Mount Zion, found the sanctuary deserted and overgrown, and cleansed it. They tore down the defiled altar, stored its stones "until a prophet should come," built a new altar of whole stones, relit the lampstand and set out the bread. On 25 Kislev 148 (December 164 BC), three years to the day after the pagan sacrifice, they dedicated the altar with songs and instruments for eight days, and the whole assembly decreed that the days be kept each year (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). The book tells of no miracle of oil; that story comes from the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 21b).

1 Maccabees presents Mattathias's killing of a Jew at the king's altar as a second Peor: "He was zealous for the law, as Phinehas had been against Zimri son of Salu" (1 Maccabees 2:26). His dying speech names "Phinehas our father," who "received the covenant of a holy priesthood" (1 Maccabees 2:54), and the hymn for Judas says he "turned anger away from Israel" (1 Maccabees 3:8), as Phinehas turned back God's rage (Numbers 25:11). The comparison gave the priestly Hasmonean family a claim to the reward of Phinehas's zeal.

In the persecution of 167 BC a thousand faithful Jews let themselves be killed in the desert rather than fight on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 2:29–38). Mattathias and his friends then decided to defend themselves if attacked on the Sabbath, though not to start a battle (1 Maccabees 2:39–41). Jubilees 50:12, from the same century, counts making war among things forbidden on the Sabbath; Josephus says Pompey used the Jews' rule of defense only to build his siege works on Sabbaths in 63 BC (Antiquities 14.63). The rabbis later taught that saving life overrides the Sabbath (Babylonian Talmud Yoma 85b).

1 Maccabees tells of Jews in Jerusalem who "made foreskins for themselves," disguising their circumcision to take part in Greek athletics (1 Maccabees 1:15). Antiochus's decree forbade circumcision; women who had their sons circumcised were killed with their babies and families (1 Maccabees 1:48, 60–61). When the revolt began, Mattathias's men circumcised by force the boys they found uncircumcised in Israel's borders (1 Maccabees 2:46).

sections.b: Antiochus's decree ordered the sacrifice of pigs and "unclean animals" (1 Maccabees 1:47). The book honors those who "steeled themselves not to eat what was unclean" and "accepted death rather than be made unclean by food" (1 Maccabees 1:62–63). 2 Maccabees tells the stories of such martyrs at length, among them Eleazar and the mother with seven sons (2 Maccabees 6:18–7:42). Daniel's refusal of the king's food (Daniel 1:8) was read in the same light.

1 Maccabees honors the dead of the persecution in a few lines: mothers killed with their babies for circumcising them, people who chose to die rather than eat unclean food, and a thousand who died in the desert rather than break the Sabbath, saying, "Let us all die in our integrity" (1 Maccabees 1:60–63; 2:29–38). Unlike 2 Maccabees, the book does not speak of their reward after death; it honors them, then shows why the living chose to fight (1 Maccabees 2:40).

1 Maccabees avoids the word God. In its Greek, Mattathias speaks of the law, the covenant and "him" (1 Maccabees 2:61), and Judas speaks of "Heaven": "To Heaven it makes no difference whether it saves by many or by few" (1 Maccabees 3:18). The people cry out "to Heaven" and bless Heaven (1 Maccabees 3:50; 4:10, 24, 55). Later copyists and translators, including the Vulgate and the KJV, often supplied "God" or "the Lord." The usage is found in Daniel 4:26 and in rabbinic phrases such as "the fear of Heaven" (Mishnah Avot 1:3).

sections.h: Judas's wars and the law of war
sections.b: 1 Maccabees tells Judas's battles in the pattern of Deuteronomy 20 and the wars of Joshua and Saul. Before Emmaus he gathers the people to fast and pray, appoints officers over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, and sends home those the law exempts: men building houses, engaged to be married, planting vineyards, or afraid (1 Maccabees 3:46–56; Deuteronomy 20:5–8). He tells his men that "strength comes from Heaven" (1 Maccabees 3:19), as Jonathan and David had said (1 Samuel 14:6; 17:47). Yet the book tells of no miracle in battle; victory comes through courage and tactics.

sections.b: 1 Maccabees and Daniel 7–12 come from the same crisis, and the book uses Daniel's language. It calls the pagan altar in the Temple an "abomination of desolation" (1 Maccabees 1:54; Daniel 11:31; 12:11), and Mattathias's last speech names Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael, saved from the flame, and Daniel, rescued from the lions (1 Maccabees 2:59–60). Most scholars read Daniel 11:21–39 as a history of Antiochus IV that 1 Maccabees 1 helps to explain.

1 Maccabees introduces Antiochus IV Epiphanes as "a sinful root" from Alexander's successors, a former hostage in Rome who became king in 175 BC (1 Maccabees 1:10). It tells of his invasion of Egypt, his robbing of the Temple and his decree against the law (1 Maccabees 1:16–51). In 165 BC, short of money, he marched east and left Lysias as regent with half the army; Lysias sent Ptolemy son of Dorymenes, Nicanor and Gorgias against Judea, and came himself the next year (1 Maccabees 3:27–4:35). The king's death in the east is told in chapter 6.

The family enters history with Mattathias son of John, son of Simeon, a priest of the line of Joarib, who moved from Jerusalem to Modein (1 Maccabees 2:1). His five sons each bore a nickname: John Gaddi, Simon Thassi, Judas Maccabeus, Eleazar Avaran and Jonathan Apphus (1 Maccabees 2:2–5). The family name, Hasmonean, does not occur in 1 Maccabees; Josephus traces it to an ancestor called Asamonaios (Antiquities 12.265). Mattathias's dying speech names Simon as a father to his brothers and Judas as commander (1 Maccabees 2:65–66), giving the later line of Simon its place from the start.
